title: Why generals need economists to win long wars
gist: Ribakova argues GDP size is a poor predictor of war-fighting capacity, citing Ukraine and Iran, and lays out a four-block research agenda (generating resources, converting them, denying them to adversaries, and staying in power). She urges economists and generals to cooperate and to measure what military spending actually delivers.

insights.claim: Non-US NATO GDP of $26 trillion versus Russia's $2 trillion is a misleading comparison, since at purchasing power parity Russia's military spending is almost the same as that of the EU and UK combined.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Use PPP-based defense spending rather than nominal GDP when assessing European deterrence.

insights.claim: Russia's economy is more than ten times Ukraine's, yet Ukraine is still fighting four and a half years into an invasion Moscow expected to finish in three days.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Mobilization and adaptation matter more than raw economic scale in long wars.

insights.claim: Iran's economy is about 1% the size of the US, yet over eight months of war it has tied down US forces, used up half to two-thirds of US missile defense interceptors that take at least five years to rebuild, and kept global energy markets hostage while driving up US inflation.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Interceptor depletion is a multi-year constraint on US defense; supports defense-industrial demand and energy-risk premia.

insights.claim: Composite capability measures such as the Composite Index of National Capability narrow gaps but measure potential rather than mobilization.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Standard power indices overstate rich-country advantage; discount them when forecasting war outcomes.

insights.claim: Economists' contributions grow as wars become long wars, attrition or asymmetric conflicts, in which economic management must be part of military strategy; converting economic power into military power determines how long each side can hold out.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Long-war duration depends on fiscal and industrial staying power, not battlefield outcomes alone.

themes.theme: Four building blocks of war economics

insights.claim: War economics can be organized into four building blocks: generating resources, converting resources into military capabilities, denying resources to an adversary, and staying in power.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist for assessing any belligerent's endurance.

insights.claim: War finance hinges on the mix of taxation, debt, money creation and external financing, with central banks acting as the financial rear by keeping payments, banks and policy predictable to preserve confidence that the state will survive.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Fiscal and monetary regime strain is a leading indicator of wartime stress.

insights.claim: Absorptive capacity acts as a multiplier on external aid: Ukraine converts allied aid into fighting power, whereas the $145 billion the US spent rebuilding Afghanistan over 20 years did not prevent its government's collapse.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Aid effectiveness depends on recipient institutions, informing judgments about sustained Ukraine support.

insights.claim: Ukraine lost roughly a quarter of its effective labor force after the 2022 invasion, but wage flexibility, remote work and hiring women and older workers limited the fall in job-matching efficiency to about 15%.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Labor-market flexibility cushions wartime mobilization shocks.

insights.claim: Prolonged reservist call-ups and the exclusion of Palestinian workers are weighing on Israel's economy.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Long mobilization imposes a measurable drag on the Israeli economy.

insights.claim: US and German incumbents built around bespoke, capital-intensive, slow-to-produce materiel resist entry of new firms when cheap drones are needed, whereas Ukraine and Iran, with few incumbents and acute scarcity, shifted quickly.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Scarcity can be an innovation advantage; favors new defense-tech entrants over incumbents in drone-type demand.

insights.claim: Russia lags Ukraine in innovation but is closing the gap and is more successful at scaling production, mostly of older, proven technology, while Ukraine's 180-plus European partnerships should help it scale.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Scale versus innovation trade-off shapes attrition dynamics.

insights.claim: Recent wars have reversed the traditional defense R&D model, with civilian technology now pulled into military use rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Dual-use commercial tech suppliers gain defense relevance.

insights.claim: Economic warfare cannot win wars alone but contributes through sanctions, blockades, strategic bombing and long-range strikes on refineries and shipping lanes, constrained by coalition size, costs, adaptation and enforcement.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Evaluate sanctions by enforcement and coalition breadth.

insights.claim: More than 40% of 2,500 components in Russian weapons used in Ukraine came from four American suppliers, per US Senate hearings.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Supplier concentration is a pressure point for export-control enforcement.

insights.claim: Iran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz shows how a much smaller economy can impose steep, far-reaching costs on a far richer adversary.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Chokepoint disruption is the main route for small-state leverage; keep an energy risk premium.

insights.claim: Narratives aimed at domestic and international audiences lower the cost of other inputs by sustaining credibility with bond markets, publics and allied militaries.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Credibility with creditors and allies is itself a war resource.

insights.claim: Coup-proofing and patronage impose deadweight loss on converting economic power into military power, because securing elite cooperation is not always what is best for the economy.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Regimes that prioritize survival over efficiency underperform their economic weight.

insights.claim: Venezuela shows regime survival differs from national capability: it survived while its oil industry decayed and offered no resistance to US intervention.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Regime durability should not be read as national strength.

insights.claim: Rather than rely on aggregate GDP or defense spending as a share of GDP, the US and Europe should use purchasing power parity and trace how funding, including allied support, becomes production, deployable capabilities and battlefield effects.
insights.speaker: Elina Ribakova
insights.so_what: Judge Western rearmament by delivered capability, not budget headline numbers.
